extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, researchers and practitioners interested in railway safety and accident causation
extracted.subtask_description: Overview and classification of railway accidents, their types, causes, contributory factors, and prevention strategies; useful for studying, reporting, and preventing train accidents. Covers both effect-based and cause-based taxonomies and common failure modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification by effects (Stockert)
rubrics_metrics.description: A classification of accidents by their effects (consequences) — e.g., head-on collisions, rear-end collisions, derailments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ludwig von Stockert (1913) proposed this approach; with minor changes it represents best knowledge. Classification by effects is a valuable aid in studying accidents to help prevent similar ones occurring in the future.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification by causes (Schneider and Mase)
rubrics_metrics.description: A classification of accidents by their causes — e.g., driver's errors, signalmen's errors, mechanical faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schneider and Mase (1968) proposed this complementary classification; together with effects-based classification it gives a more systematic and complete understanding of accidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collision types and primary human causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Several types of train collision such as head-on, rear-end and side collisions. In freight trains the three most common causes are failure to obey or display signals, speeding, and violation of mainline rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collisions are rare but the most severe type of train accident, causing on average 21 casualties in passenger trains. Misuse of signals accounted for over half of the total damage costs; analysis should therefore emphasise signal compliance and rule adherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derailment causes and speed factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Derailments are a common accident type (apart from grade crossings). Most common causes include broken rails and welds, track geometry, bearing failure, and wheel failures. Speed influences derailment type: human error common below 25 mph, mechanical issues peak at higher speeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because majority of derailments are caused by rail problems, rail maintenance and track geometry inspection are among the most effective prevention strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Driver error and human factors (including automation-related)
rubrics_metrics.description: Driver error (disobeying signals, speeding, disregarding mainline rules) is the most dangerous cause of passenger train derailments and collisions. Human factors are most prevalent in the 81–100 mph range. Automation-related human factors (unsupervised use of automated systems, ignorance of alarms) have also caused accidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigations include technological controls such as positive train control to prevent speeding and signal disregard; human-factors analysis should consider both manual and automation interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signalman error
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors caused by signalmen include allowing two trains into the same occupied block section and incorrect operation of signals, points or token equipment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signal operations and procedures, training, and equipment reliability are key areas to evaluate to prevent these errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rolling stock failure
rubrics_metrics.description: Issues with rolling stock include poor design, poor maintenance, undetected damage, overloading or freight not adequately secured, and fires starting from motors, electric cables or equipment, leaking fuel or cooling oil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should examine design standards, maintenance regimes, inspection effectiveness, load-securing practices, and electrical/fuel system safety to identify and mitigate rolling stock failure risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil engineering failure
rubrics_metrics.description: Failures of railway civil engineering include track (permanent way) faults, bridge and tunnel collapses, and poor track or junction layout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infrastructure inspection, design adequacy, and maintenance of track, bridges and tunnels are critical to preventing these failures; layout/design reviews can reduce vulnerability to accidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other people — accidental and deliberate interference
rubrics_metrics.description: Other people can cause accidents accidentally (e.g., accidental track obstruction by road or construction vehicles) or deliberately (rail sabotage, deliberate track obstruction, intentional damage to infrastructure, intentional misalignment of switches). Related causes include level crossing misuse, trespass, riot, and terrorism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Risk assessments should include human and malicious threats, protections at level crossings, trespass prevention, surveillance and security measures, and procedures to detect/mitigate sabotage or deliberate misalignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural causes include track obstruction or damage by landslides, avalanches, floods, trees; fog or snow that obscure signals or the current position of the train; and wet leaves making tracks slippery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Environmental monitoring, weather-related operating restrictions, vegetation management, and drainage/landslide mitigation are prevention measures to consider when evaluating natural-cause risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other accident forms (fires, hazardous releases, assaults, pedestrian collisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Other forms of train accident include fires, explosions and release of hazardous chemicals (including sabotage/terrorism), people falling from trains (including train surfing), collisions with people on tracks, and attacks such as shootings or bombings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preparedness for hazardous-material incidents, onboard safety measures, platform and trespass prevention, and security countermeasures are relevant evaluation dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory factors affecting severity
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributory factors listed include strength of rolling stock, presence of fire hazards or dangerous goods in the train or nearby road vehicles, effectiveness of brakes, and inadequate rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of accident risk and potential severity should include vehicle crashworthiness, hazardous goods policies, braking system performance, and adequacy of operating rules/regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systemic / socio-technical perspective and value of systematic investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern safety research treats railway systems as complex socio-technical systems in which accidents arise from interactions among multiple components rather than a single cause. Systematic investigation and classification over 150 years has led to an excellent safety record compared with road transport.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations and prevention strategies should adopt a systems view, looking at interactions among human, technical, organizational and regulatory factors; long-term systematic study and classification are recommended to improve safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevention and mitigation strategies (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of effective prevention include positive train control to prevent speeding and signal disregard, and rail maintenance and track geometry inspection to prevent derailments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating safety measures, consider technological controls (PTC), maintenance practices, inspection regimes, infrastructure improvements, and rule/procedure adequacy; quantify impact where possible (e.g., reduction of signal-related collisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of severity and frequency metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: The article cites quantitative metrics (e.g., collisions account for about one in 24 crashes; derailments ~18% of accidents 1996–2017; collisions average 21 casualties in passenger trains) as part of analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should use frequency and severity statistics to prioritise interventions and understand which accident types cause the most harm or costs.
